title: Ensure continued business justification
blurb: Explain what 'ensure continued business justification' requires, from the first decision to start until the benefits are confirmed.
question: A new law forces a council to upgrade its bus stops. A board member says the project needs no business case because it is compulsory. Is that consistent with PRINCE2?

teach.h: A valid reason to start, and to keep going
teach.body: Formally: a PRINCE2 project must have a justifiable reason to start, and that justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project. If the project can no longer be justified, it should be stopped. In plain English: never start a project you cannot justify, and keep asking 'is this still worth it?' all the way through.

The justification is what keeps the project aligned with the benefits being sought and the business objectives it should contribute to. Organizations that lack this rigour see projects carry on with few real benefits, or with only a loose link to strategy. The justification is usually documented in a business case, which the executive is accountable for.

values: Which way of complying is best value?

teach.h: At a decision point: is the project still justified?

root.label: Board reviews the updated business case

teach.caption: Stopping a project that is no longer justified is a success of the principle, not a failure of the project.

teach.h: What applying the principle looks like
items: Justification exists and is approved before work starts (outline, then full business case).
It is revalidated at each stage boundary and when big issues or risks arise.
Requests for change weigh the extra benefit against the extra cost and risk.
Every party, suppliers included, needs its own balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify taking part.
After closure, the business reviews whether the benefits justified the investment and records lessons.

teach.h: Worked scenario: the bus stop upgrade
teach.body: Fernbrook District Council must make 40 bus stops accessible under new regulations. Executive Anita Rao is told no business case is needed. Project manager Tomasz Novak disagrees: he compares doing the minimum (raised kerbs only) with a fuller upgrade adding real-time displays, and documents costs, benefits and risks. At the end of stage one, steel prices rise; the board checks the updated business case and confirms the chosen option is still the best value.

teach.text: Classic trap: 'it's compulsory, so we don't need a business case'. Ensure continued business justification still applies: you justify the option chosen to meet the obligation. Second trap: the principle is not a one-off check at the start. 'Continued' means revalidated throughout.

items: A justifiable reason to start, kept valid and revalidated throughout the project.
If it is no longer justified, the project should be stopped.
Usually documented in the business case; the executive is accountable for it.
Compulsory projects still justify the chosen option; suppliers need their own justification too.
v7 name: 'ensure continued business justification' (6th edition had no 'ensure').

summary: You can now explain what ensure continued business justification requires at the start, throughout and after a project. You can also recognize that compulsory projects still justify their chosen option and that stopping an unjustified project applies the principle.

A.q: Which statement describes the 'ensure continued business justification' principle?
options: A justifiable reason to start must exist and stay valid
The business case is approved once, before initiation
Benefits must be realized before the project can close
Each stage must deliver products of measurable value
A.why: There must be a justifiable reason to start the project, and the justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout (manual 2.1).

whyNot.1: Justification is revalidated throughout, not approved once and left.
whyNot.2: Most benefits are realized after closure; the principle does not require them before closing.
whyNot.3: This mixes in focus on products; the principle is about the project remaining justified.

A.q: A project is required by new legislation. How does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle apply?
options: It does not apply because compliance is mandatory
The chosen option for complying must be justified
The business layer replaces the business case
The justification is checked at closure instead
A.why: Even compulsory projects need justification of the chosen option, so that the best-value way of complying is selected.

whyNot.0: The principle applies to every PRINCE2 project, compulsory ones included.
whyNot.2: The business layer commissions the project; it does not replace the business case.
whyNot.3: Justification is checked throughout, not deferred to closure.

A.q: At a stage boundary the updated business case shows that the project can no longer be justified. What does the principle say should happen?
options: The project manager raises an issue report
The next stage goes ahead with lower tolerances
The benefits are moved into the next project
The project should be stopped
A.why: If the justification is no longer valid, the project should be stopped (manual 2.1); the board triggers a premature close.

whyNot.0: An issue report records an issue; it does not address a project that is no longer justified.
whyNot.1: Changing tolerances does not make an unjustified project worthwhile.
whyNot.2: Moving benefits elsewhere does not deal with this project's lack of justification.

B.q:
Which two statements about ensure continued business justification are correct?
1. The justification must be revalidated throughout the project.
2. Suppliers need their own justification for taking part.
3. Compulsory projects are exempt from the principle.
4. The business case is fixed once the project is authorized.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout (1), and all parties, including suppliers, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks for their involvement (2).

whyNot.1: Statement 3 is false: compulsory projects justify the chosen option.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: the business case is maintained and updated at each stage end.
whyNot.3: Both are false: no project is exempt, and the business case is kept up to date.

B.q: What usually documents the business justification for a PRINCE2 project?
options: The project brief
The business case
The project plan
The benefits management approach
B.why: The justification is usually documented in a business case: estimated costs against expected benefits, offset by risks.

whyNot.0: The project brief contains the outline business case, but the justification itself sits in the business case.
whyNot.2: The project plan provides costs and timescales that feed the business case.
whyNot.3: The benefits management approach defines how benefits will be measured and reviewed.

B.q: A request for change would add a new feature. Applying 'ensure continued business justification', what should be considered?
options: Whether the team has spare capacity this stage
Whether the feature fits the original product list
Whether the extra benefit outweighs cost and risk
Whether the senior user has asked for it formally
B.why: Justification can change, so a change must be weighed: does the extra benefit justify the extra cost and risk?

whyNot.0: Capacity matters for planning, but it does not test justification.
whyNot.1: Fit with the product list relates to scope; justification is about benefit versus cost and risk.
whyNot.3: Who raised the request does not decide whether the change is justified.

C.q: Why does the principle say 'continued' business justification?
options: Because the business case is created again for each stage
Because the executive must sign the business case every month
Because benefits reviews happen continuously during delivery
Because the justification must stay valid and be revalidated
C.why: Justification is not a one-off check: it must remain valid throughout and is revalidated, for example at each stage boundary.

whyNot.0: One business case is maintained and updated, not recreated each stage.
whyNot.1: There is no monthly signing rule; checks happen at decision points and when issues arise.
whyNot.2: Most benefits reviews happen after closure, planned in the benefits management approach.

C.q: Which role is accountable for the business case, and when does the board formally check it before delivery starts?
options: Executive; when authorizing the project
Senior user; when authorizing the project
Project manager; when assessing progress
Executive; when authorizing closure
C.why: The executive is accountable for the business case. The board checks the full business case when authorizing the project, before delivery stages start.

whyNot.1: The senior user specifies and realizes benefits; the executive owns the business case.
whyNot.2: The project manager prepares and maintains it, but is not accountable for it.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable, but the board checks the business case long before closure, starting with authorizing initiation.

C.q: After closure, how is the 'ensure continued business justification' principle still served?
options: The project board meets to approve the final stage plan
The business reviews whether the benefits were realized
The project manager updates the outline business case
The team managers produce a final checkpoint report
C.why: After the project, the business reviews whether benefits materialized enough to warrant the investment (planned in the benefits management approach).

whyNot.0: Stage plans are approved during the project, not after closure.
whyNot.2: The outline business case belongs to starting up; the project manager's role ends at closure.
whyNot.3: Checkpoint reports cover work package progress during a stage.

reteach.title: Would you still buy it today?
reteach.question: Imagine buying a car on monthly payments that you can cancel at any point. At each payment, what question should you ask?

blocks.body: You would only start paying if the car was worth it. If your job moved and you no longer needed it, you would stop. PRINCE2 treats every project the same way: there must be a good reason to start, and at every decision point the board asks whether the reason still holds. If it does not, the project stops. Even an unavoidable purchase (say, a legally required safety repair) still needs the best-value option.

blocks.h: Every decision point asks the same thing

blocks.text: Stopping a project that is no longer justified is the principle working, not a failure.

explain.body: A justifiable reason is needed to start, and it must remain valid and be revalidated throughout. If it is lost, the project should be stopped.

test.q: When must a PRINCE2 project have a valid business justification?
options: At the start and throughout
At the start of initiation
At each project closure review
When an exception is raised
test.why: There must be a justifiable reason to start and it must remain valid throughout the project.

whyNot.1: Justification is needed before initiation and must stay valid afterwards too.
whyNot.2: Checking at closure is too late to steer the investment.
whyNot.3: Exceptions trigger a check, but justification is needed all the time.

explain.body: A project required by law or regulation still needs justification: of the option chosen to comply. The best-value way of meeting the obligation is selected and documented.

test.q: A regulator requires a bank to upgrade its fraud checks. What must the business case justify?
options: The decision to obey the regulator
The cost of the work, not its benefits
The option chosen to meet the rule
The regulator's original reasons
test.why: Compulsory projects still need business justification, of the chosen option.

whyNot.0: Obeying the regulator is not optional; the open choice is how to comply.
whyNot.1: Justification balances benefits against costs and risks; here it is the chosen option that is justified.
whyNot.3: The regulator's reasons are outside the project's business case.

explain.body: As the project goes on, costs, risks and the environment change, so the justification evolves. What the project delivers must stay consistent with it, which is why changes are weighed against benefit, cost and risk.

test.q: In which business case technique step does the project manager update the business case at the end of each stage?
options: Develop
Check
Maintain
Confirm
test.why: Maintain: at each stage end the PM updates the business case with progress and latest forecasts.

whyNot.0: Develop creates the outline and full business case.
whyNot.1: Check assesses whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.
whyNot.3: Confirm assesses whether benefits have been or will be realized, mostly after closure.

explain.body: All parties, including suppliers, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify their own involvement. A supplier's justification is separate from the customer's business case.

head: Party
Its justification
rows: Its own benefits, costs and risks of taking part

test.q: Which statement about suppliers and business justification is correct?
options: Suppliers rely on the customer's business case
Suppliers need their own reason to take part
Suppliers justify their work at closure instead
Suppliers' justification is held by the executive
test.why: All parties need a balance of benefits, costs and risks for their own justification for involvement (manual 2.1).

whyNot.0: The customer's business case justifies the customer's investment, not the supplier's.
whyNot.2: Justification is needed throughout, not deferred to closure.
whyNot.3: The executive owns the customer's business case, not the supplier's justification.
